title: Viruses – Introduction to Virology
sub: Lecture 3 · RNDr. Jiří Černý, Ph.D. · 16 Oct 2026
blurb: The lecture opens with a review of molecular and cell biology (DNA vs RNA, RNA structure levels, amino-acid classes, protein structure levels, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells).
lede: The lecture opens with a review of molecular and cell biology (DNA vs RNA, RNA structure levels, amino-acid classes, protein structure levels, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells). It then asks what viruses are (non-cellular obligate intracellular parasites; the "virocell" idea), and shows how small (~120 nm, coronavirus) and genetically simple (2–2,500 genes) they are. The history runs from polio in Ancient Egypt, variolation in China, Jenner and Pasteur to TMV and the discovery of viruses. Then come virus structure (capsid, capsomers, envelope, nucleocapsid; icosahedral, filamentous and head-tail shapes; HIV as an example) and classification (by structure, host, nucleic acid type, the Baltimore classification and taxonomy). The six steps of replication follow, then pathogenesis, ecological cycles, vectors, and beneficial viruses.

questions.e: Uncoating releases the genome inside the cell; release is budding, exocytosis or lysis. (Slides: p. 62)

items.a: Class VI, ssRNA with reverse transcription.

items.n: Where do RNA and DNA viruses usually replicate?
items.a: RNA viruses in the cytoplasm, DNA viruses in the nucleus (with exceptions).

items.n: Example of a beneficial virus from the lecture?
items.a: A virus in a fungus in a plant gives the plant heat tolerance (three-way symbiosis); also phages.
